precepts.text: For unto me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt.
precepts.point: Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal. They claimed they were the masters; did they do that? No. They lived in the big house while we lived in the outhouse, and we never got the forty acres and the mule. So they showed themselves hypocrites and impostors. The verse ends: knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
More on these servants: “For unto me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.”

The children of Israel are servants, and they are his servants, the ones he brought out of Egypt. That is who the servants of Colossians are, and why the masters must remember they “also have a Master in heaven”: the servants belong to the Lord.

They changed the narrative and flipped the script, inserting themselves into the scriptures where they are not. Where they are, Leviticus shows it right after: “Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you”, and “they shall be your bondmen for ever”. They were originally our possession, but we sinned against our God and became their possession. Don’t worry: it is going to go back to the way it is supposed to be.

precepts.text: Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession. Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron. Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
precepts.point: And ye shall take them as an inheritance for your children after you, to inherit them for a possession; they shall be your bondmen for ever. We were originally to have them as servants, but we sinned against our God and became their possession. It is going to go back to the way it is supposed to be.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
Leviticus 25:46 says of the heathen bondmen, “ye shall take them as an inheritance for your children after you”. Hold that, and hear Psalm 2: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.”

The Lord is saying, don’t worry, it is going back to that. He is going to give us the heathen for our inheritance. Meaning what? We are going to own them. That is what it is saying right there. We were their possession, but they were originally our possession; we sinned against our God and became theirs, and it is going to go back to the way it is supposed to be.

“Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel.” If they don’t want to get right, boom, upside the head. “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.”

So the inheritance of Leviticus 25:46 and the inheritance of Psalm 2:8 are the same: the heathen given to Israel for an inheritance and a possession, ruled with a rod of iron.

precepts.why:
Leviticus 25:46 says “they shall be your bondmen for ever”. For how long? Forever. Esau thinks he can change his judgment. No. No. You cannot change it. God said it, it is in writing, it is stamped. So that means you are going back into slavery.

Isaiah shows it coming to pass: “the house of Israel shall possess them in the land of the Lord for servants and handmaids: and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors.” For servants and handmaids, because that is the role the Lord gave them, and for how long? Forever. The judgment of Leviticus 25:44-46 cannot be undone.

precepts.point: The glory of Lebanon, the fir, pine, and box, shall beautify the place of my sanctuary; Lebanon and its famous trees belong to the Israelites. The sons of them that afflicted thee shall come bending, and all that despised thee shall bow at the soles of thy feet and call thee the city of the Lord, the Zion of the Holy One of Israel. note.label: Prophesy From Pain to Peace

precepts.why:
Isaiah 60 is the true third temple. Solomon built the first; Zerubbabel and Joshua rebuilt the second during the Persian captivity; and here is the third. “And the sons of strangers shall build up thy walls”. The third temple is built by the other nations, because the other nations will be our slaves. That makes some nervous, but that is what it says.

Here is the law behind it, for anyone struggling: “Moreover of the children of the strangers that do sojourn among you, of them shall ye buy, and of their families that are with you, which they begat in your land: and they shall be your possession.” Those are the same strangers Isaiah speaks of in verse 10. We shall own them, possess them as slaves.

“And ye shall take them as an inheritance for your children after you, to inherit them for a possession; they shall be your bondmen for ever”. For how long? For ever. Then: “but over your brethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigour”.

So when Isaiah says “their kings shall minister unto thee”, it is that law being carried out in the kingdom. God was angry with us and smote us, and we went into slavery: “in my wrath I smote thee”. Then: “but in my favour have I had mercy on thee”: that is why he sent Christ. Now the order is turned back to what the law always said: the strangers serve, and Israel is not ruled with rigour.

precepts.text: When ye come into the land, the land shall keep a sabbath unto the Lord.
precepts.point: The Sabbath of the land is built on the seventh-day Sabbath.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
Exodus 23 gives the seventh year release: work the land six years, “But the seventh year thou shalt let it rest and lie still; that the poor of thy people may eat”. Leviticus 25 lays out the same law: “And the Lord spake unto Moses in mount Sinai, saying, Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye come into the land which I give you, then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the Lord”. He is telling us what to do when we enter the land, and we entered the land under Joshua, not under Moses.

“Six years thou shalt sow thy field, and six years thou shalt prune thy vineyard, and gather in the fruit thereof; But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land”. Don't farm the land that year. “That which groweth of its own accord of thy harvest thou shalt not reap”: whatever grows on its own during the seventh year, that is what you eat. “And the sabbath of the land shall be meat for you; for thee, and for thy servant, and for thy maid, and for thy hired servant, and for thy stranger that sojourneth with thee”.

The seventh year release is built on the seventh-day Sabbath. Exodus 23 says it right after the land: “Six days thou shalt do thy work, and on the seventh day thou shalt rest”. The Sabbath goes for the land as well; when you have property, you let your land rest.

And the question everybody asks is answered in verse 20: “What shall we eat the seventh year? behold, we shall not sow, nor gather in our increase: Then I will command my blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall bring forth fruit for three years”. The sixth year covers you for three years. Brothers and sisters say, I got to work on the Sabbath because that's my money day. Then you don't believe what we just read. That was the same question in verse 20, and God answered it: work six, rest on the seventh, and he provides.

precepts.text: The land shall not be sold for ever, for the land is mine.
precepts.point: Land was priced by the number of harvests left until the Jubilee, because the land is the Lord's.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
The whole Jubilee rests on this: “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.” Israel could sell the use of a field, but never the field itself, because the land belongs to the Most High. He is the owner, and he decides its proper use. That is why nobody in Israel was to heap up land for himself: it never really belonged to them.

That is also why the price of land was worked by the harvests left until the Jubilee. “According to the multitude of years thou shalt increase the price thereof, and according to the fewness of years thou shalt diminish the price of it: for according to the number of the years of the fruits doth he sell unto thee.” More years means more crops, so a higher price; one year left means one harvest, so the price has to be less. What was bought was the crops, not the land. And in the middle of it: “Ye shall not therefore oppress one another; but thou shalt fear thy God”.

Look at how black people chip each other and undercut each other today. That is why we have to come back to the Bible and apply these basic principles. When our own try to oppress one another in business, our people go to the Chinese man instead. God says don't oppress one another.

The Most High even provided for the year they could not farm. “What shall we eat the seventh year?” “Then I will command my blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall bring forth fruit for three years.” That answers everyone who says they have to break the Sabbath to make their money. It is connected to the seventh-day Sabbath, where what was needed was baked beforehand and laid up for the seventh; here it is the sixth year he increases. It is all spiritual.

Read on: “And in all the land of your possession ye shall grant a redemption for the land.” If a brother waxed poor and sold some of his possession, a kinsman could come and redeem what he had to sell away. If none could, and he later had the means himself, he counted the years and restored the overplus, the extra. And if he could not, the land stayed in the hand of the buyer only “until the year of jubile”, and then he returned to his possession, money or no money. Every fifty years it all goes back.

There is a spirit in the land. The woman who came to Esdras was Jerusalem, and the Most High wanted us to see that there is a connection between the people and the land. So when the trumpet sounds on the Day of Atonement in the fiftieth year and liberty is proclaimed, every man returns to his possession and his family, because the land was never anybody's to keep but the Lord's.

precepts.text: Bondmen and bondmaids shall be of the heathen round about you.
precepts.point: Bondmen from the heathen round about are a possession for ever, but not so over your brethren.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
After the law for a poor brother comes the distinction: “Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you; of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids.” Your bondmen and bondmaids shall be of the heathen, the other nations. A bondservant is like chattel slavery, and that is what Israel was never to make of a brother.

Keep reading: “Moreover of the children of the strangers that do sojourn among you, of them shall ye buy, and of their families that are with you, which they begat in your land: and they shall be your possession.” Now the word stranger is talking about the heathen, as the verse above explained. “And ye shall take them as an inheritance for your children after you, to inherit them for a possession; they shall be your bondmen for ever”. For how long? For ever. They got passed down from generation to generation, to your son and your daughter. The other nations were not released in the Jubilee; they remained slaves. That is what God said.

Then the stress on but: “but over your brethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigour.” There is the distinction. Your brother who waxes poor and is sold to you serves “as an hired servant, and as a sojourner”, what we call a job today; back then they called you a servant. He serves until the Jubilee, and then “shall he depart from thee, both he and his children with him, and shall return unto his own family”. “For they are my servants, which I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: they shall not be sold as bondmen.” “Thou shalt not rule over him with rigour; but shalt fear thy God.” Rigour is hardship: busting him in the head, whooping him. Don't do that.

The word stranger in this chapter does not always mean another race. The stranger of verse 35, “though he be a stranger, or a sojourner”, is a brother of another tribe, like Judah living in the land of Simeon, a stranger there. Numbers 16:40 shows it: “no stranger, which is not of the seed of Aaron, come near to offer incense before the Lord”. Anyone not of the seed of Aaron, Judah, Benjamin, Manasseh, Ephraim, Gad, Reuben, was called a stranger. But in verses 44 and 45 the stranger is the heathen round about.

So the Jubilee's liberty was for Israel. The poor brother went free; the bondmen of the heathen did not. “For unto me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt”. Verse 55 tells you plain: the Israelites are God's servants. Everybody on the planet is not God's servants.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
When a brother waxed poor and sold himself to a sojourner or stranger, it was not the end of him: “After that he is sold he may be redeemed again; one of his brethren may redeem him”. This is not saying we sold ourselves to the other nations. It is another tribe. A man of Judah whose land is jacked up goes among the tribe of Gad and says, I'm poor, I need to work for you, help me. Esau will use this chapter and try to cause confusion with that word stranger, saying see, the other nations. No. That is about Israel.

“Either his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him; or if he be able, he may redeem himself.” A kinsman could buy him back, and if he came into some money while he was working, he could say, I don't need this anymore, and redeem himself.

The price was reckoned the same way as the land: “from the year that he was sold to him unto the year of jubile: and the price of his sale shall be according unto the number of years, according to the time of an hired servant shall it be with him.” The price is according to the years left from now to the Jubilee. “If there be yet many years behind”, the price of his redemption is higher; “if there remain but few years unto the year of jubile”, it is lower. It is the same concept as the land.

“And as a yearly hired servant shall he be with him: and the other shall not rule with rigour over him in thy sight.” That goes back to verse 43. “And if he be not redeemed in these years, then he shall go out in the year of jubile, both he, and his children with him.” That goes back to verse 41.

Why? “For unto me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.” A poor brother of Israel is never a bondservant for ever. He is the Lord's servant, he can always be redeemed, and in the Jubilee he goes free with his children.

When a brother waxed poor and sold himself to a sojourner or stranger, it was not the end of him: “After that he is sold he may be redeemed again; one of his brethren may redeem him”. This is not saying we sold ourselves to the other nations. It is another tribe. A man of Judah whose land is jacked up goes among the tribe of Gad and says, I'm poor, I need to work for you, help me. Esau will use this chapter and try to cause confusion with that word stranger, saying see, the other nations. No. That is about Israel.

“Either his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him; or if he be able, he may redeem himself.” A kinsman could buy him back, and if he came into some money while he was working, he could say, I don't need this anymore, and redeem himself.

The price was reckoned the same way as the land: “from the year that he was sold to him unto the year of jubile: and the price of his sale shall be according unto the number of years, according to the time of an hired servant shall it be with him.” The price is according to the years left from now to the Jubilee. “If there be yet many years behind”, the price of his redemption is higher; “if there remain but few years unto the year of jubile”, it is lower. It is the same concept as the land.

“And as a yearly hired servant shall he be with him: and the other shall not rule with rigour over him in thy sight.” That goes back to verse 43. “And if he be not redeemed in these years, then he shall go out in the year of jubile, both he, and his children with him.” That goes back to verse 41.

Why? “For unto me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.” A poor brother of Israel is never a bondservant for ever. He is the Lord's servant, he can always be redeemed, and in the Jubilee he goes free with his children.

precepts.text: I am the Lord which brought you out of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan; that is the land of the promise.
precepts.point: The land given to Abraham and Isaac was promised to Jacob and his seed: the land of Canaan, which is northeast Africa, the land the Most High named when He brought Israel out of Egypt.

note.label: Genesis 35: Bethel and the Twelve Sons of Israel

precepts.why:
“I am the Lord your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan, and to be your God.”

That is the land of the promise. “And the land which I gave Abraham and Isaac, to thee I will give it, and to thy seed after thee”: the land of Canaan, which is northeast Africa, the land the Most High named when He brought Israel out of Egypt.

precepts.text: The bondmen are of the heathen and the strangers, a possession for ever; but over your brethren the children of Israel ye shall not rule with rigour.
precepts.point: The law sets the order: bondmen and bondmaids are to be of the heathen round about and of the strangers that sojourn among you; they are a possession and an inheritance for the children. But over the brethren, the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigour.

note.label: Exodus 12: The Lord's Passover

precepts.why:
“And a mixed multitude went up also with them”. The mixed multitude that left Egypt with Israel were not to be among the children of Israel as rulers. The law sets the order of who is who.

“Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you; of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids. Moreover of the children of the strangers that do sojourn among you, of them shall ye buy, and of their families that are with you, which they begat in your land: and they shall be your possession. And ye shall take them as an inheritance for your children after you, to inherit them for a possession; they shall be your bondmen for ever”. The bondmen and bondmaids are of the heathen round about and of the strangers that sojourn among Israel; they are a possession and an inheritance for the children, for ever.

“but over your brethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigour.” The brethren are not ruled with rigour by one another, and the strangers that went up with Israel are not the rulers. That is the order for the mixed multitude that came out of Egypt.

precepts.text: Thy brother that is waxen poor and sold unto thee shall not serve as a bondservant, but as an hired servant, unto the year of jubile.
precepts.point: Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
“And if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant: But as an hired servant, and as a sojourner, he shall be with thee, and shall serve thee unto the year of jubile”.

The brother that waxes poor and is sold is not to be compelled to serve as a bondservant. He is an hired servant and a sojourner with you, and he is not to be ruled over harshly. That is the spirit in which the Hebrew servant of Exodus 21 serves his six years.

precepts.text: If thy brother be waxen poor, though he be a stranger or a sojourner, relieve him; take no usury of him, and lend him not thy victuals for increase.
precepts.point: This is twofold, and first and foremost the stranger is your brother from a different area, our own people. Leviticus 25 shows it: if thy brother be waxen poor, though he be a stranger or a sojourner, sojourn meaning travel, thou shalt relieve him that he may live with thee. A brother of another tribe who falls on hard times and travels down to live with you is that stranger; neither vex him nor oppress him, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
This is twofold, and first and foremost the stranger is your brother from a different area, our own people. Leviticus 25 shows it: “And if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee.” Thy brother is called a stranger or a sojourner, and sojourn means travel. A brother of another tribe who falls on hard times and travels down to live with you is that stranger.

How he is to be treated: “Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee. Thou shalt not give him thy money upon usury, nor lend him thy victuals for increase.” Neither vex him nor oppress him, “for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

precepts.text: Thy brother waxen poor is called a stranger or a sojourner, so the stranger of this law is your own brother outside his allotment.
precepts.point: The bondmen laws show the contrast in how the word stranger is used. The bondmen and bondmaids were to be of the heathen round about, and in that context the children of the strangers sojourning among you are the heathen, a possession and an inheritance; but over your brethren the children of Israel ye shall not rule with rigour. Then the sojourner or stranger that waxeth rich by thee returns to the Israelite stranger, for the bondservant of the heathen did not wax rich.

note.label: Leviticus 19: Ye Shall Be Holy, for I the Lord Your God Am Holy

precepts.why:
Who is the stranger of this law? “if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee.” Thy brother waxen poor is called a stranger or a sojourner.

So the stranger here is an Israelite of another tribe sojourning outside the allotment of his own tribe. A man of Judah dwelling in the land of Benjamin is a stranger to that land, because that was not the allotment the Most High gave him.

When your brother the stranger falls into decay, relieve him and let him sojourn with you; give him work to deliver him out of his low state until he can stand again. That is loving him as thyself.

precepts.text: In the bondmen context the stranger is the heathen round about, but over your brethren the children of Israel ye shall not rule with rigour.
precepts.point: The bondmen laws show the contrast in how the word stranger is used. The bondmen and bondmaids were to be of the heathen round about, and in that context the children of the strangers sojourning among you are the heathen, a possession and an inheritance; but over your brethren the children of Israel ye shall not rule with rigour. Then the sojourner or stranger that waxeth rich by thee returns to the Israelite stranger, for the bondservant of the heathen did not wax rich.

note.label: Leviticus 19: Ye Shall Be Holy, for I the Lord Your God Am Holy

precepts.why:
The bondmen laws show the contrast in how the word stranger is used. “Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you.” And “of the children of the strangers that do sojourn among you, of them shall ye buy, and of their families that are with you, which they begat in your land: and they shall be your possession.”

In that context the strangers sojourning among you are the heathen, taken “as an inheritance for your children after you”, “bondmen for ever.” But the line is drawn: “over your brethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigour.”

So the word stranger can mean the heathen round about, or it can mean your own brother outside his allotment; the context tells which. The stranger of Leviticus 19:33-34, loved as thyself and as one born among you, is the brother.

precepts.text: The stranger who waxes rich by thee is again the Israelite stranger, for the bondservants of the heathen were a possession and did not wax rich.
precepts.point: The bondmen laws show the contrast in how the word stranger is used. The bondmen and bondmaids were to be of the heathen round about, and in that context the children of the strangers sojourning among you are the heathen, a possession and an inheritance; but over your brethren the children of Israel ye shall not rule with rigour. Then the sojourner or stranger that waxeth rich by thee returns to the Israelite stranger, for the bondservant of the heathen did not wax rich.

note.label: Leviticus 19: Ye Shall Be Holy, for I the Lord Your God Am Holy

precepts.why:
“And if a sojourner or stranger wax rich by thee, and thy brother that dwelleth by him wax poor, and sell himself unto the stranger or sojourner by thee.” Here the word returns to the Israelite stranger.

The bondservants of the heathen were a possession and an inheritance; they did not wax rich. A stranger who waxes rich by thee and to whom a poor brother can sell himself is an Israelite sojourning outside his own tribe’s land. That is the stranger Leviticus 19:33-34 commands you not to vex, but to love as thyself.

precepts.text: Ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you; buy is interchangeable with redeem, and no nation redeemed Israel out of this captivity.
precepts.point: Redeem and buy are interchangeable words here: his kin come to redeem it meaning to buy it back. This is the prime example to reference for the curse that says no man shall buy you: no man shall redeem you. The other nations never came to say, we want to redeem Israel out of slavery and set them back to freedom; Israel has been in slavery for hundreds of years and no nation did that.

note.label: Leviticus 25: The Sabbath of the Land and the Year of Jubile

precepts.why:
“If thy brother be waxen poor, and hath sold away some of his possession, and if any of his kin come to redeem it, then shall he redeem that which his brother sold.” Redeem and buy are interchangeable words here: his kin come to redeem it, meaning to buy it back.

This is the prime example to reference for the curse: “there ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you.” No man shall buy you means no man shall redeem you.

The other nations never came to say, we want to redeem Israel out of slavery and set them back to freedom. Israel has been in slavery for hundreds of years and no nation did that. The kinsman redeemer of Leviticus 25 never came for us; that is the curse fulfilled.

precepts.text: Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself; brother, neighbour, and children of thy people are the same.
precepts.point: I am the Lord your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan. The Most High is not the God of everybody: to bring Israel out He judged Egypt, and to give Israel Canaan He cast out the seven nations, greater and mightier than Israel, delivered them before Israel to be smitten, with no covenant and no mercy shewed, during that time period.

note.label: Leviticus 25: The Sabbath of the Land and the Year of Jubile

precepts.why:
“if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner.” The word stranger does not always mean a heathen; sometimes it is your own brother sojourning away from his land, and the context of the verse tells you which.

Thy brother is thy neighbour and the children of thy people: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him. Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” Brother, neighbour and children of thy people all mean the same thing. Relieving thy brother waxen poor is loving thy neighbour as thyself.

precepts.text: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee; since thou wast precious in my sight, I have loved thee, therefore will I give men for thee. A ransom secures the safe exit of the victim; the Most High gave Egypt and Ethiopia their own lives to bring Israel out.
precepts.point: I am the Lord your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan. The Most High is not the God of everybody: to bring Israel out He judged Egypt, and to give Israel Canaan He cast out the seven nations, greater and mightier than Israel, delivered them before Israel to be smitten, with no covenant and no mercy shewed, during that time period.

note.label: Leviticus 25: The Sabbath of the Land and the Year of Jubile

precepts.why:
“I am the Lord your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt.” The Most High is not the God of everybody. To bring Israel out He judged Egypt: “I am the Lord thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee.”

A ransom secures the safe exit of the victim. The Most High gave Egypt and Ethiopia their own lives to bring Israel out. “Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee: therefore will I give men for thee, and people for thy life.” That is the God speaking in Leviticus 25:38.

precepts.text: Seven nations greater and mightier than Israel were cast out and delivered before Israel to be utterly destroyed, with no covenant made and no mercy shewed; that is how the Most High gave the land of Canaan.
precepts.point: I am the Lord your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan. The Most High is not the God of everybody: to bring Israel out He judged Egypt, and to give Israel Canaan He cast out the seven nations, greater and mightier than Israel, delivered them before Israel to be smitten, with no covenant and no mercy shewed, during that time period.

note.label: Leviticus 25: The Sabbath of the Land and the Year of Jubile

precepts.why:
He brought Israel out of Egypt “to give you the land of Canaan, and to be your God.” This is how He gave it: “When the Lord thy God shall bring thee into the land whither thou goest to possess it, and hath cast out many nations before thee, the Hittites, and the Girgashites, and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations greater and mightier than thou.”

“And when the Lord thy God shall deliver them before thee; thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them.” Seven nations greater and mightier than Israel, cast out and delivered before Israel to be smitten, with no covenant and no mercy shewed, during that time period.

He judged Egypt to bring Israel out and cast out the seven nations to give Israel Canaan. The Most High is the God of Israel, not the God of everybody.

precepts.text: If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve, and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing; the brother sold to thee goes out at the release.
precepts.point: For they are my servants, which I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: they shall not be sold as bondmen. Thou shalt not rule over him with rigour, but shalt fear thy God; deal with him properly, for the Most High judges both the poor man and the one he serves.

note.label: Leviticus 25: The Sabbath of the Land and the Year of Jubile

precepts.why:
“If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve: and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing.” That is the release the brother sold to thee goes out at. He is not compelled to serve as a bondservant; he is with thee as an hired servant and as a sojourner, and when his time is up he departs, he and his children with him, and returns to his own family and to the possession of his fathers.

“If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself: if he were married, then his wife shall go out with him.” Nothing he came in with is kept back from him at his release.

That seventh year of release is that servant’s jubile. It runs from the year he was taken: a servant taken in 2012 goes out free in 2019, and one taken in 2019 goes out free in 2026.

The reason is in the verses themselves: they are the Most High’s servants, which He brought forth out of the land of Egypt, and they shall not be sold as bondmen. So thou shalt not rule over him with rigour, but shalt fear thy God, and deal with him properly, for the Most High judges both the poor man and the one he serves.

precepts.text: The strangers sojourning among Israel were to be their bondmen and bondmaids.
precepts.point: They had just seen the Lord consume the complainers in the uttermost parts of the camp, and they went back and did the same thing. We are the same people today; there is nothing new under the sun, and these things were written aforetime for our learning, so we can read them and refuse to do as they did.

note.label: Numbers 11: Beware of Murmuring

precepts.why:
The mixed multitude that fell a lusting were the other nations among Israel, and the law tells what they were for. “Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you; of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids. Moreover of the children of the strangers that do sojourn among you, of them shall ye buy, and of their families that are with you, which they begat in your land: and they shall be your possession.”

The strangers sojourning among Israel were to be the bondmen and bondmaids of Israel. Instead, the nations sprinkled in the camp led the lusting, and the children of Israel followed the very people they were to rule over, and wept for the fish, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic of Egypt.

precepts.text: The heathen round about are bought for bondmen and taken for a possession for ever; that is what Edom becomes to Israel.
precepts.point: Out of Jacob shall come he that shall have dominion: that is the one who cometh from Edom with dyed garments from Bozrah, glorious in his apparel, traveling in the greatness of his strength, which is the whole host of heaven, thousands upon thousands of angels. The day of vengeance is in his heart, for though Israel serves out her punishment in captivity, Esau went overboard and kept laying on punishment when our iniquity had an end.

note.label: Numbers 24: A Star out of Jacob and the Latter Days

precepts.why:
“And Edom shall be a possession, Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies; and Israel shall do valiantly.” Edom is nowhere named in the matter of Balak and Balaam in these chapters, but the Lord made sure Edom was written into the prophecy. The law of bondmen shows what a possession is.

“Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you; of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids.” Of the strangers that sojourn among you and their families, “they shall be your possession. And ye shall take them as an inheritance for your children after you, to inherit them for a possession; they shall be your bondmen for ever: but over your brethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigour.”

The heathen round about are bought for an inheritance, bondmen for ever, though over our own brethren we do not rule with rigour. That is what Edom becomes to Israel: a possession. But for Esau that servitude is not for ever, because Esau is the only nation on the earth with an expiration date; the rest of the nations go into servitude for ever, but the Lord can only bear with Esau so much longer.

precepts.text: If thy brother be waxen poor, then thou shalt relieve him, yea, though he be a stranger or a sojourner, that he may live with thee.
precepts.point: The stranger of this commandment is thy brother fallen into decay, whom thou shalt relieve, not the nations Israel was commanded to drive out.

note.label: Deuteronomy 10: What Doth the Lord Require of Thee

precepts.why:
“And if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee.” Here the law says it plainly: the stranger and the sojourner to be relieved is thy brother, waxen poor and fallen in decay. That is the stranger of this commandment, whom the Lord loves in giving him food and raiment, and whom Israel is told to love.

It is not the nations Israel was commanded to drive out. It is thy brother fallen into decay, the brother who became a stranger when the northern kingdom was cut off, and who is coming back into the covenant. Thou shalt relieve him, that he may live with thee; and remember, “ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

precepts.text: The land keeps a sabbath unto the Lord: six years thou shalt sow thy field, but in the seventh year is a sabbath of rest unto the land.
precepts.point: Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it again, but that which is thine with thy brother thine hand shall release. The seven year release stands on the sabbath of the land already given in Leviticus 25.

note.label: Deuteronomy 15: The Year of Release and the Hebrew Servant

precepts.why:
The seven year release stands on the sabbath of the land already given in Leviticus 25. “When ye come into the land which I give you, then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the Lord. Six years thou shalt sow thy field, and six years thou shalt prune thy vineyard, and gather in the fruit thereof; But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land, a sabbath for the Lord: thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard.”

Six years of sowing and a seventh of rest is the same count as “At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release.” In the year the land rests, every creditor releases what he lent his neighbour, and “shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the Lord’s release.”

Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it again, but that which is thine with thy brother thine hand shall release.

precepts.text: If thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor and be sold unto thee; the Hebrew sold himself to his brother when he fell poor.
precepts.point: The reason given is memory: remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the Lord thy God redeemed thee.

note.label: Deuteronomy 15: The Year of Release and the Hebrew Servant

precepts.why:
Who is the Hebrew man or Hebrew woman sold unto thee? Leviticus 25 says: “And if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant”. The Hebrew sold himself to his brother when he fell poor.

When people say slavery was taking place in Africa among us, it was not slavery like we suffered: it was people among us that fell poor and sold themselves to their brothers, the very case this law and Leviticus 25 govern.

He served six years, and in the seventh year he went free, and not empty: furnished liberally out of the flock, the floor, and the winepress, with some of the flock, the corn, and the wine. He cannot go out poor the way he came in; that shows you the Most High is a good God. And the reason given is memory: remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the Lord thy God redeemed thee.

precepts.text: A brother sold to a stranger may be redeemed by his kin; in this captivity no kinsman can redeem you, for all Israel is sold into bondage together.
precepts.point: There ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you: buy means redeem. Under the servitude laws a poor brother sold to a stranger could be redeemed by his uncle, his uncle's son, or any of his kin; but in this captivity none of your brothers can redeem you, because they are in bondage right along with you, as verse 29 already said: no man shall save thee.

note.label: Deuteronomy 28: The Blessings and the Curses That Identify Israel

precepts.why:
“and there ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you.” Buy means redeem. Under the servitude laws, if a brother waxed poor and sold himself unto a stranger, “After that he is sold he may be redeemed again; one of his brethren may redeem him: Either his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him; or if he be able, he may redeem himself.”

That is the law of buying back a brother. But in this captivity no man shall buy you: none of your brothers can redeem you, not your uncle, not your uncle's son, not any of your kin, because they are in bondage right along with you. All Israel was sold into bondage together, and there was nobody left free to pay the price.

precepts.text: Thy bondmen and bondmaids shall be of the heathen round about you; the other nations were made to be Israel's servants, but over your brethren ye shall not rule with rigour.
precepts.point: This is according to the law of the Most High pertaining to other nations. If you just read the Old Testament, there was no equality among the nations, and there is still no equality among nations: they were made for a certain purpose. The reason they are not in that purpose now is because we have sinned and failed, and one day Israel will rise again to put them back in their rightful places.

note.label: Joshua 9: The Gibeonite Deception and the Weight of an Oath

precepts.why:
“let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation”. Hewers of wood and drawers of water means slaves. This is according to the law of the Most High pertaining to other nations: “Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you”, and of “the children of the strangers that do sojourn among you”; “they shall be your bondmen for ever”, an inheritance for your children after you. The Gibeonites were heathen dwelling among Israel, so the oath to let them live did not set them free; it set them to serve.

If you just read the Old Testament, there was no equality among the nations, and there is still no equality among nations: they were made for a certain purpose. The one line drawn is among ourselves: “but over your brethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigour.” The reason the nations are not in their purpose now is because we have sinned and failed, and one day Israel will rise again to put them back in their rightful places.

precepts.text: The bondmen and bondmaids of Israel shall be of the heathen round about and of the children of the strangers that sojourn among you; they shall be your possession. When we get into the kingdom this order will be in place.
precepts.point: Ruth fell on her face and asked, Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger? She acknowledged what she was to Israel: a stranger.

note.label: Ruth 2: Gleaning in the Field of Boaz

precepts.why:
Ruth called herself a stranger in Israel, and the law shows what the place of the stranger is. “Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you; of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids. Moreover of the children of the strangers that do sojourn among you, of them shall ye buy, and of their families that are with you, which they begat in your land: and they shall be your possession.”

“And ye shall take them as an inheritance for your children after you, to inherit them for a possession; they shall be your bondmen for ever: but over your brethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigour.” The bondmen and bondmaids of Israel are of the heathen round about and of the children of the strangers that sojourn among us; they are Israel's possession, but over our brethren we do not rule with rigour.

When we get into the kingdom this order will be in place. Ruth, a stranger, fell on her face before Boaz because she understood it.

precepts.text: Bondmen and bondmaids are to be taken of the heathen round about, so the tribute of bondservice was lawful.
precepts.point: Of the children of Israel Solomon made no bondmen, but they were men of war, his servants, princes, captains, and rulers of his chariots and horsemen; instead of enslaving his own people he built them up and gave them positions.

note.label: 1 Kings 9: The Most High Appears to Solomon a Second Time

precepts.why:
“Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you; of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids.” Bondmen and bondmaids are to be taken of the heathen round about.

So when Solomon levied a tribute of bondservice on “all the people that were left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, which were not of the children of Israel”, it was lawful by the law.

“But of the children of Israel did Solomon make no bondmen: but they were men of war, and his servants, and his princes, and his captains, and rulers of his chariots, and his horsemen.” Instead of enslaving his own people, he built them up and gave them positions.

precepts.text: The land was not to be sold forever, for it belonged to the Most High and was held as a family inheritance.
precepts.point: Naboth refused because the land was the inheritance of his fathers. He could not simply hand off an inheritance that was given to him.

note.label: 1 Kings 21: Naboth's Vineyard and the Judgment on Ahab

precepts.why:
“The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.” The land belonged to the Most High and was held as a family inheritance.

So the armed men left the captives and the spoil, and the men named by name clothed the naked, shod them, gave them “to eat and to drink, and anointed them, and carried all the feeble of them upon asses, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brethren”.
